what: a JS-style `const` local binding inside a function.

ideal.title: Local bindings use {c:let}; {c:const} is a top-level declaration

provide.how: Inside a body parse.utu reads `const` as a name expression and fails expecting ";" at `pi`. A statement starting with a top-level-only keyword (const, mem, fn, struct, enum) should fail with a hint naming it; this one suggests `let`.

feasibility.mechanism_check: `const` starting a statement inside a body matches the table entry JS `const` local -> `let`.

what: a test block named with a bare word instead of a string.

ideal.title: A test's name is a string: {c:test "addition"}

provide.how: parse.utu string_lit() calls fail() at `addition`, so nothing is wanted ("unexpected 'addition'"). Call fail_wanting(Tok.String) so the text reads "expected a string", and offer the quoted word as the fix.

feasibility.mechanism_check: A test name has one form, a string; quoting the user's word `addition` gives `test "addition"`.

what: a method receiver written as an untyped first parameter (Python/Rust habit).

ideal.title: A method names its receiver in bars: {c:fn Rect.area |self| ()}

provide.how: parse.utu reads `self` as a parameter and fails expecting ":" at ")". Add a syntax-hint table consulted when the parse fails (parse.utu fail_wanting already knows the furthest token): match the failing token and its neighbours against known habits and record a hint id beside parse_error_wanted, which diag.utu turns into the title, labels, note, and fix. Pattern: a method declaration (`fn Type.name`) whose first parameter is an untyped `self`.

feasibility.mechanism_check: A method receiver has one form, `fn Type.name |self| (params)`; the untyped first parameter `self` moves into bars and the list is left empty.

what: an @es DSL block is never closed with `\/`.

ideal.title: The {c:@es} block opened here is never closed with {c:\/}

provide.how: lex.utu finds no "\/" for the DslBody and emits Tok.Error at the "/", so the text is "unexpected character '/'". The lexer should emit a dedicated error at the "@" with the opener's span; diag.utu adds an arm for it.

feasibility.changed: Dropped the fix: where the DSL body was meant to end is a guess (the `;` could be part of the JS).

what: a `\\` multiline string's terminating ';' written on the same line as its text.

ideal.title: The {c:;} on a {c:\\} line is part of the string text
notes: End the string with {c:;} on a line of its own after the last {c:\\} line.

provide.how: diag.utu already special-cases this (semicolon_in_multiline) in the ParseError text. Point the primary span at the ";" inside the last \\ line instead of the "}", keep "}" as related, and move the hint into a note.

what: a using declaration that forgets the word `from`.

ideal.title: {c:using console} needs {c:from} before the module

provide.how: parse.utu checks the optional `from` with is_kw, so it is never recorded as wanted, and expect(p, Tok.Semi) says "expected ';'". Record kw_wanted + Kw.From at that position (fail_wanting) so the set reads "'from' or ';'"; the module-shaped token after it selects the fix.

feasibility.mechanism_check: Of the expected set {from, ;} after `using console`, only `from` lets `std:Console` parse, so the insertion is unique.

what: the last match arm has no trailing comma.

ideal.title: Every match arm ends with {c:,}, including the last

provide.how: parse.utu's arm loop expects Tok.Comma and fails at "}". For a wanted ";" (or ":" / ","), diag_start/diag_end should point at tok_end of the token before the failing one (ptok[pos-1]) instead of the next token, which is often on the next line. The better change is in the grammar: let the loop end at "}" after the last arm, and this file then compiles.

feasibility.mechanism_check: The arm loop wants exactly {,} after `~> "many"`; inserting it lets the "}" close the match.

what: an else branch written without braces.

ideal.title: An {c:else} branch is a block, even for one value

provide.how: parse.utu expects "{" after `else` and fails at `0`; the text is right. The fix wraps the tokens up to the statement's ";" in a block and adds the closing ";".

feasibility.mechanism_check: `else expr;` has one correct form, `else { expr; };`; the expression `0` runs to the statement's ";".

what: digit-group underscores in an integer literal (`1_000_000`).

ideal.title: Integer literals cannot contain {c:_} digit separators

provide.how: lex.utu reads `1` as Tok.Int and `_000_000` as a word, so the parser fails expecting ";" there. The lexer should notice a digit run followed directly by "_" and a digit and emit an invalid-number error spanning the whole run (or simply accept and strip the underscores).

feasibility.mechanism_check: `1_000_000` matches the table entry for digit-group underscores, which are dropped.

what: two array literal elements are not separated by a comma.

ideal.title: A comma is missing between the array elements {c:2} and {c:3}

provide.how: The array literal loop tests `is(p, Tok.Comma)` without fail_wanting, so wanted_text gives only "']'". Record Tok.Comma at that position so the set is "',' or ']'", and when the failing token can start an expression, title it as a missing comma.

feasibility.mechanism_check: Of the expected set {",", "]"} at `3`, only "," lets `3` parse as the next element.

what: a C-style `/* ... */` block comment.

ideal.title: utu has only {c://} line comments; {c:/*} does not start one

provide.how: lex.utu emits "/" and "*" and parse.utu fails at "/" ("unexpected '/'"). The lexer can recognise "/*" (adjacent) and emit a dedicated error spanning to "*/" when it is on the same line.

feasibility.mechanism_check: `/* ... */` on one line matches the table entry for a C block comment -> `// ...`.

what: a tuple destructured with parentheses `let (q, r) = ...` instead of `let .{q, r}`.

ideal.title: A tuple is taken apart with a leading dot, not with parentheses

provide.how: parse.utu's let fails at "(" ("unexpected '('"). Add a syntax-hint table consulted when the parse fails (parse.utu fail_wanting already knows the furthest token): match the failing token and its neighbours against known habits and record a hint id beside parse_error_wanted, which diag.utu turns into the title, labels, note, and fix. Pattern: `let (`; names never resolve after a parse error, so the hint stands alone.

feasibility.changed: Removed the related mark on divmod's return type: this is a parse error, so names never resolve and the callee is not known.
feasibility.mechanism_check: A tuple pattern has one form, `let .{q, r}`; the user's names stay.

what: an empty `${}` hole in a template string.

ideal.title: A template hole needs an expression inside it

provide.how: The parser fails at the TemplateTail token ("} items`"), and found_text prints its raw text. When the failing token is a template middle or tail right after a template head, report an empty-hole error spanning "${}".

feasibility.changed: Dropped the fix and the "perhaps n" mark: choosing what goes in the hole invents the expression.

what: an inline closure written with the type keyword `fun` instead of `cl`.

ideal.title: {c:fun} names a function type; write an inline closure with {c:cl}

provide.how: parse.utu reads `fun(` as a type in expression position and fails expecting ")" at ":". Add a syntax-hint table consulted when the parse fails (parse.utu fail_wanting already knows the furthest token): match the failing token and its neighbours against known habits and record a hint id beside parse_error_wanted, which diag.utu turns into the title, labels, note, and fix. Pattern: `fun (` at an expression start followed by a block.

feasibility.mechanism_check: An inline closure has one form, `cl(params) T { ... }`; replacing `fun` with `cl` at the expression start keeps the rest.

what: a helper function declared inside another function's body.

ideal.title: Functions cannot be nested; {n:square} must be a closure or top-level

lines.text: fn sum_of_squares(a: I32, b: I32) I32 {
fn square(x: I32) I32 { x * x; }

notes: Move {n:square} above {n:sum_of_squares} as its own {c:fn}, or bind it as a closure with {c:let square = cl(...)}.

provide.how: parse.utu reads `fn` as a name (identifier() never checks is_keyword_id) and fails expecting ";" at `square`. A statement starting with `fn` should fail with a hint; the enclosing function's header is on hand in the body parser as a related span.

feasibility.changed: Dropped the closure fix: moving `square` to the top level is equally good, so neither edit is the one; the note now names both.

what: a JS/Rust-style `\u{1F600}` code-point escape.

ideal.title: {c:\u} takes four hex digits; U+1F600 needs a surrogate pair
notes: A code point above U+FFFF is written as two {c:\u} escapes.

provide.how: strings.utu decode_string sets bad_escape at the "\u", but the diag span is the whole string node. Use bad_escape for the span (to the closing brace when one follows), and when the braces hold a hex code point, compute its surrogate pair for the fix.

feasibility.mechanism_check: `\u{1F600}` has one correct form: the code point above U+FFFF is computed into its surrogate pair `\uD83D\uDE00`.

what: a high surrogate escape with no low surrogate after it.

ideal.title: {c:\uD83D} is a high surrogate, but no low surrogate follows

marks.label: needs a low surrogate after it

notes: A high surrogate (D800 to DBFF) must be followed by a low one, {c:\uDC00} to {c:\uDFFF}.

provide.how: strings.utu decode_string returns false on the surrogate paths without setting bad_escape, so check.utu bad_literal falls back to unsupported() ("not supported yet"). Set bad_escape and a reason code (lone high, lone low, bad pair) there, and give InvalidEscape one message per reason in diag.utu.

what: an unknown escape `\d` (regex habit) in a string literal.

ideal.title: {c:\d} is not an escape in a utu string
notes: The escapes are {c:\n} {c:\t} {c:\r} {c:\b} {c:\f} {c:\uXXXX} and an escaped quote, backslash, backtick, or {c:$}.
Write {c:\\d} for a backslash followed by d, or {c:d} alone.

provide.how: strings.utu decode_string turns any other `\c` into `c` (its else arm). That arm should set bad_escape to the backslash unless c is a quote, backslash, backtick, or "$", so bad_literal reports InvalidEscape with the escape as span.

feasibility.changed: Dropped the fix: `\\d` and plain `d` are both plausible; a note names them.

what: a Windows path with single backslashes, so `\n` and `\p` are escapes.

ideal.title: {c:\p} is not an escape; a Windows path needs doubled backslashes

marks.label: and this one is a newline

notes: Write {c:\\} for each backslash in a path.

provide.how: Same check as an unknown escape in decode_string. When the string also holds a valid escape followed by letters (\n then "ew"), record it as a related span, since that one is silently a newline.

feasibility.changed: Dropped the fix: doubling also rewrites the valid `\n`, which picks what the user meant; the note gives the rule.

what: a C-style `\0` NUL escape.

ideal.title: {c:\0} is not an escape; write {c:\u0000} for NUL

provide.how: decode_string turns "\0" into "0" through its else arm. With the unknown-escape check, a digit after the backslash gets the \u0000 suggestion.

feasibility.mechanism_check: The table maps the C escape `\0` to `\u0000`.

what: an integer literal too large for a U8 binding.

ideal.title: {f:300} does not fit in a {e:U8}, which holds 0 to 255
notes: Use a wider type such as {c:U16}, or a value up to 255.

provide.how: check.utu fits() checks only I32, U32, M32, and the sign of I64, so a U8 literal of 300 compiles and traps. Add the ranges for I8, U8, I16, U16 and U64, include the range in the IntegerOutOfRange text, and pass the node the expected type came from (the let annotation) as a secondary span.

feasibility.changed: Dropped the U16 fix: a wider type or a smaller value are both possible; a note names them.

what: a big literal with no annotation defaults to I32 and overflows.

ideal.title: {f:3000000000} is too big for an {e:I32}, the default integer type
notes: With no annotation an integer literal is an {e:I32}; annotate the binding, for example {c:let big: I64}.

provide.how: check.utu int_literal falls back to I32 when nothing is expected, and fits() reports IntegerOutOfRange. Pass a flag (expect < 0) so diag.utu adds the default-type note, the range in the label, and the annotation fix on the let.

feasibility.changed: Dropped the annotation fix: it makes line 5's `big.to_i64()` an error (fixcheck: other); the note now says what to do.

what: a negative literal assigned to an unsigned type.

ideal.title: {f:-1} does not fit in a {e:U32}, which has no negative values
notes: For all bits set write {c:0xFFFFFFFF}; for a negative value use a signed type.

provide.how: int_literal reports on the literal node, so the caret skips the minus. Report on the negation node instead (int_literal knows `negate`), add the annotation as a type-origin span, and suggest the all-ones hex form for -1.

feasibility.changed: Dropped the 0xFFFFFFFF fix: it invents what -1 meant; a note names the options.

what: a literal argument too big for an I32 parameter.

ideal.title: {f:5000000000} is too big for {n:ms}, an {e:I32} parameter
notes: Widen {n:ms} to {c:I64} if it needs values this large.

provide.how: The call checker passes the parameter type as `expect` to int_literal but not where it came from. Record the parameter declaration node with the expected type (type origin) and pass it in diag_c so the renderer adds the parameter as an expected span.

what: a 32-bit all-ones hex mask in an I32 context.

ideal.title: {f:0xFFFFFFFF} is too big for an {e:I32}
notes: On an {e:I32}, {c:-1} has every bit set; or make {n:x} a {c:U32}.

provide.how: fits() reports; the expected type is the other operand's (x). Record the operand's declaration as the type origin, print the max in hex when the literal was written in hex, and suggest -1 when the literal is all ones.

feasibility.changed: Dropped the `-1` fix: making `x` a U32 is equally good; the note names both.

what: one element of a byte array literal does not fit in U8.

ideal.title: {f:256} does not fit in a {e:U8} element, which holds 0 to 255

provide.how: Same missing U8 range in check.utu fits(); the array literal passes the element type as `expect`, so once fits() knows U8 the element is reported. The annotation becomes the type-origin span.

what: a literal beyond even I64's range.

ideal.title: {f:99999999999999999999} is too big even for an {e:I64}

provide.how: int_value accumulates digits in an I64 and wraps silently, so fits() sees 7766279631452241919. The lexer (or int_value) must flag overflow while reading the digits, and fits() must report any flagged literal regardless of type.

what: a tuple type used as a function parameter.

ideal.title: A parameter cannot be a tuple; tuples are only function results
notes: Pass the values as separate parameters.

provide.how: validate.utu reports TupleMisplaced with variant 0, but diag.utu's code name has no case for it and falls back to "type-mismatch". Give it its own code, and pick the title by the position (parameter, let, field) the validator already knows.

feasibility.changed: Dropped the fix: it invents names a and b and leaves line 4 using `p` (fixcheck: other); the note no longer points at line 4.

what: a local binding annotated with a tuple type.

ideal.title: A local cannot hold a tuple; take it apart instead

lines.text: fn divmod(a: I32, b: I32) .{I32, I32} { .{a / b, a % b}; }

notes: Take it apart with a tuple pattern in the {c:let}, one name per value.

provide.how: Same TupleMisplaced site in validate.utu. When the initializer is a call, the callee's return type node (resolved later in check) can be added as a related span.

feasibility.changed: Dropped the fix: q and r are invented names; a note gives the form.

what: a struct field with a tuple type.

ideal.title: A struct field cannot be a tuple
notes: Use one field per value, or a struct.

provide.how: validate.utu knows the tuple type sits in a struct field but diag.utu gives the parameter wording ("take it apart with let"). Pass the position as a variant and give the field case its own text and note.

feasibility.changed: Removed the invented field names lo and hi from the note.

what: a function returning a tuple that contains another tuple.

ideal.title: A tuple cannot hold another tuple
notes: Flatten it into one tuple, both in the type and where the result is built.

provide.how: The message is right; only the code is wrong (falls back to "type-mismatch" in diag.utu). The validator has the inner and outer tuple nodes, so the flattened type is easy to print.

feasibility.changed: Dropped the fix: it leaves the nested value on line 4 (fixcheck: other); the note no longer names a line the validator does not track.

what: a closure type whose result is a tuple.

ideal.title: A closure cannot return a tuple
notes: A closure is a JS function with one result; use a {c:fn} or {c:fun} value instead.

provide.how: The text is right; give TupleMisplaced its own code in diag.utu and move the reason into a note.

what: an array literal built from tuple-returning calls.

ideal.title: Tuples cannot be stored in an array

lines.text: fn divmod(a: I32, b: I32) .{I32, I32} { .{a / b, a % b}; }

notes: Take each result apart with {c:let} first and store the parts.

provide.how: data.utu check_array_lit reports TupleMisplaced (variant 3) on the array literal; it should point at the first tuple element instead. The element is a call whose callee is known there, so its return type node can be passed in diag_c as a related span.

what: an array type whose element is a tuple.

ideal.title: An array cannot hold tuples
notes: Use two arrays, or an array of a struct with two fields.

provide.how: validate.utu reports the tuple type twice, in the signature and in the body; report the first only (one per function, or drop reports whose type text repeats). Use the array wording rather than the "function result" one, since the parent is an array type.

what: destructuring a value that is not a tuple.

ideal.title: {n:total} returns an {f:I32}, not a tuple to take apart

lines.text: fn total(a: I32, b: I32) I32 { a + b; }

provide.how: control.utu reports TupleLet with the value's type; diag.utu has no code for it ("type-mismatch"). Give it its own code and, when the value is a call, pass the callee's return type node as the found span.

what: destructuring a three-value tuple into two names.

ideal.title: This tuple has 3 values, but only 2 names are given
notes: Give the pattern one name per value.

provide.how: control.utu has the tuple type and the pattern; add the callee's return type as an expected span.

feasibility.changed: Dropped the fix: the name `count` is invented; a note asks for one name per value.

what: destructuring a struct as if it were a tuple (JS object destructuring habit).

ideal.title: {f:Point} is a struct, not a tuple; read its fields instead
notes: Bind the struct to a name and read its fields {c:x} and {c:y}.

provide.how: control.utu reports TupleLet with the struct type; the struct's declaration node is at hand (ty_decl), so pass it as a related span and give a struct-specific note listing its fields.

feasibility.changed: Removed the invented binding name p from the note; it names the real fields.

what: an optional chain `?.` used as the value of a let.

ideal.title: {c:?.} cannot give {n:second} a value when {n:head.next} is null
notes: {c:?.} only guards a whole statement; use {c:promote} or {c:orelse} to make a value.

provide.how: misc.utu check_statement reports OptionalOutsideStatement only when the statement's value is used (expect non-void); a let whose initializer holds a `?.` is guarded and silently skipped, leaving `second` null. Report when the leftmost optional is inside a let initializer; the optional field's declaration becomes a related span.

feasibility.changed: Dropped the promote fix: it invents the capture name and the default "none".

what: an optional chain `?.` as a function's final (result) expression.

ideal.title: {c:?.} cannot be the result of {n:second_name}; {n:head.next} may be null
notes: Use {c:promote} or {c:orelse} to say what the result is when it is null.

provide.how: misc.utu check_statement already reports this; diag.utu gives it the "type-mismatch" code. Give it its own code, add the return type as the expected span.

feasibility.changed: Dropped the promote fix: it invents the capture name and the default ""; a note names promote/orelse.

what: an optional chain `?.` used inside an if condition.

ideal.title: {c:?.} in a condition skips the whole {c:if} when {n:head.next} is null
notes: Use {c:promote head.next} to say what happens when it is null.

provide.how: check_statement guards the whole if statement because its leftmost optional is in the condition, so the if is silently skipped. Report OptionalOutsideStatement when the optional is inside an if/while condition (or any operand), not only when it is the statement's value.

what: an optional chain `?.` in a return statement's value.

ideal.title: {c:?.} cannot be returned; {n:head.next} may be null
notes: Use {c:promote} or {c:orelse} to say what is returned when it is null.

provide.how: misc.utu check_base reports it; same code as for a block value.

feasibility.changed: Dropped the promote fix: it invents the capture name and the default ""; a note names promote/orelse.

what: two `export lib` blocks in one entry file.

ideal.title: A file has one {c:export lib}; this is a second one
notes: Merge the functions into the first {c:export lib}.

provide.how: resolve.utu check_entry_surface reports `lib`, the earlier one. Report `item` (the duplicate) and pass `lib` in diag_c, which diag.utu turns into a related span.

what: two `export main` entry points in one file.

ideal.title: A file has one {c:export main}; this is a second one
notes: Keep one entry point, or rename this one to a plain {c:fn}.

provide.how: Same as two libs: check_entry_surface should report `item` with `main` in diag_c as a related span.

what: both `export lib` and `export main` in one entry file.

ideal.title: A file exports either a lib or a main, not both
notes: {c:export main} makes a program and {c:export lib} a library; keep one.

provide.how: check_entry_surface reports on `lib`; report on the later of the two and pass the other in diag_c as a related span.

what: `&{ ... }` with no type annotation, so its struct type is unknown.

ideal.title: This {c:&} literal has no struct type to build
notes: An {c:&} literal takes its struct from the expected type; annotate the binding or name the struct.

provide.how: data.utu check_implicit_init reports ImplicitStructInit, and diag.utu has no text arm for it, so the user sees the bare kind name. Add the text; split on why (no expected type, a non-struct, an enum); and search the structs in scope for one whose field names match the literal's, for the related span.

feasibility.changed: Dropped the fix: annotating `p: Point` and writing `Point { ... }` are equally good; the note names both.

what: `&{ ... }` where the expected type is a number, not a struct.

ideal.title: An {c:&} literal builds a struct, but {n:total} is an {e:F64}

provide.how: Same ImplicitStructInit site; diag.utu needs the expected type (pass it in diag_a) and the annotation as a type-origin span.

feasibility.changed: Dropped the fix: replacing the literal with its field value deletes user code and guesses intent.

what: `&{ ... }` where the expected type is an enum (which variant is ambiguous).

ideal.title: An {c:&} literal cannot build the enum {e:Shape}; name the variant

provide.how: Same site; when the expected type's decl is an enum, pick the variant whose field names match the literal (did-you-mean over the variants) and add it as a related span and as the fix.

feasibility.mechanism_check: Matching the literal's field set {r} against the variants of Shape: Circle {r} matches exactly, Square {side} does not, so `Circle` is the unique variant.

what: `&{ ... }` passed to a generic-typed parameter (a struct type cannot be inferred from T).

ideal.title: This {c:&} literal has no struct type to build
notes: An array literal takes its element type from its elements, so the first element must name its struct.

provide.how: data.utu check_array_lit infers the element type with type_only(first element, -1), whose reports are discarded; it gets Ty.Error and returns error_value() silently, so the program compiles and traps. When elem is Error because an element is an implicit init with no expected type, check_array_lit must report ImplicitStructInit on that element (and the did-you-mean over struct fields applies).

feasibility.changed: Dropped the fix: naming the struct and annotating `xs: Array[Point]` are equally good; the note covers it.

what: an imported file has a syntax error (missing ';' in lib/broken_shapes.utu).

ideal.title: The imported {n:broken_shapes.utu} has a syntax error: {c:let y} needs a {c:;}
notes: Fix it in that file; the errors about {n:shapes} here go away with it.

provide.how: validate.utu reports the module's ParseError after the entry file's resolve errors ("Module 'shapes' not found", "Unknown variable 'shapes'"). When an imported file fails to parse, report its ParseError first and suppress the unknown-type and unknown-variable reports that name its module; the using node becomes a related span. For a wanted ";" (or ":" / ","), diag_start/diag_end should point at tok_end of the token before the failing one (ptok[pos-1]) instead of the next token, which is often on the next line.

what: Helper for 90_error_in_imported_file.utu: it has a syntax error on purpose (missing ';' after the let).

ideal.title: The {n:let y} statement needs a {c:;} at its end

provide.how: Checked on its own it reports "expected ';', got 'y'" on line 5. For a wanted ";" (or ":" / ","), diag_start/diag_end should point at tok_end of the token before the failing one (ptok[pos-1]) instead of the next token, which is often on the next line.

feasibility.mechanism_check: The statement parser wants exactly {;} after `x * x` before a new statement; inserting it lets `y;` parse.

what: a DSL block written without its DSL name (`@/\ ... \/` instead of `@es/\ ... \/`).

ideal.title: {c:@} needs a DSL name before its body, such as {c:@es}

provide.how: parse.utu fails at the DslBody token with nothing wanted, and found_text gives "a DSL body", making "unexpected a DSL body". The DSL rule should fail_wanting(Tok.Word) after "@", and diag.utu should word the found-side as a noun phrase that reads after "unexpected" (or "found a DSL body"); a hint names the common DSLs.

what: two string literals side by side with no `+` between them (C-style concatenation).

ideal.title: Strings are joined with {c:+}, not by writing them side by side
notes: Join them with {c:+}, or separate two arguments with {c:,}.

provide.how: parse.utu fails expecting ")" at the second string. Add a syntax-hint table consulted when the parse fails (parse.utu fail_wanting already knows the furthest token): match the failing token and its neighbours against known habits and record a hint id beside parse_error_wanted, which diag.utu turns into the title, labels, note, and fix. Pattern: a string token right after a string token.

feasibility.changed: Dropped the `+` fix: a "," (two arguments) parses too, so the edit is not unique; a note names both.

what: a doc-comment written as a bare string at the top level (Python docstring habit).

ideal.title: A bare string cannot stand at the top level of a file
notes: Doc comments are written with {c:///}.

provide.how: wutu_parse.utu reports this via wutu_fail at the #; the fix is a character swap at that offset.

feasibility.mechanism_check: A `#` at the start of a Wutu statement is the shell/Python comment spelling; the table entry # → // rewrites it.

what: a text statement without its semicolon

ideal.title: Expected {c:;} after the text {f:"Hello"}

provide.how: wutu_parse.utu fails at the token after the statement (the }); move the span back to the statement just read, which the parser has.

feasibility.mechanism_check: After the text statement "Hello" the Wutu parser expects exactly `;`; inserting it before } lets the parse continue.

what: a CSS declaration without its semicolon before the next one

ideal.title: The CSS declaration {f:padding: 1rem} has no semicolon

marks.label: read as part of the value

provide.how: wutu_parse.utu reads a CSS value up to ";" across newlines, so the next declaration is swallowed. When a value contains a newline followed by something that is_css_property accepts with ":", fail at the end of the first line (docs/wutu.md already says this is an error).

feasibility.mechanism_check: With the new newline rule, the value `1rem` ends at the line end where only `;` is expected.

what: a made-up element name without a hyphen

ideal.title: {f:card} is not an HTML element; custom elements need a hyphen
notes: For a styled box, write {c:div.card}; for a custom element, {c:my-card}.

provide.how: wutu_parse.utu reports at the head with length 1; span the whole word. The div.card rewrite is a fixed rule.

feasibility.changed: Dropped the div.card fix: div.card and my-card are two equal options (both in the note).

what: an Emmet-style class-only head (.card) expecting a div

ideal.title: {f:.card} has no tag; class-only heads don't create elements
notes: Write a tag before the class, as in {c:div.card}.

provide.how: wutu_parse.utu:775 fails at the dot; the fix inserts div before it.

feasibility.changed: Dropped the div.card fix: the tag is a choice (div, span, ...); the note shows div.card as an example.

what: two sibling root elements in one template

ideal.title: A template has one root element, but this one has two
notes: Wrap the siblings in one element, such as a {c:section}, or use a component.

provide.how: wutu_parse.utu knows both roots when it fails; point at the second head and add the first as related (both offsets are in the same body).

what: a template whose root is a text node

ideal.title: A template's root must be an element, not text

provide.how: Already reported at the text; widen the span to the statement and add the wrapping fix.

feasibility.changed: Dropped the wrap-in-p fix: the element is a choice.

what: children inside a void element (img)

ideal.title: {f:img} is a void element and can't have children
notes: For an image description, set the {c:alt} attribute.

provide.how: wutu_parse.utu reports at the img head; point at the first child instead (it is the token that triggered the check). The alt suggestion is specific to img and text children.

feasibility.changed: Dropped the alt fix: turning the child into an attribute is a guess; the note keeps the alt hint.

what: an attribute that the tag does not have (href on div)

ideal.title: {f:div} has no attribute {f:href}
notes: {c:href} is an attribute of link elements such as {c:a} and {c:area}.

provide.how: wutu_parse.utu reports at the attribute; it knows the element head, so a related span and an element-for-attribute table (href → a, src → img) give the fix.

feasibility.changed: Dropped the div→a fix: it edits the element line and picks a new element; the note states which elements have href.

what: an HTML-style onclick string attribute

ideal.title: Events are written {e:on click}, not as an {f:onclick} attribute
notes: Write the handler as an {c:on click} block with utu code inside.

provide.how: Already reported at the attribute; the fix rewrites onX = "code" as on X { code; } (the string is the handler body).

feasibility.changed: Dropped the on click fix: it treats a JavaScript string as utu code (fixcheck: Unknown variable go).

what: the old $[...] interpolation syntax

ideal.title: Wutu no longer writes {f:$[…]}; text is {e:= expr;}
notes: For an attribute, write {c:name = expr;}; for a property, {c:.prop = expr;}.

provide.how: Raised at the $; the long text splits into a short title and a note, and the fix unwraps the bracket.

feasibility.mechanism_check: The old text interpolation $[expr]; has one current form, = expr; so $[title]; becomes = title;.

what: a misspelled CSS property (colr)

ideal.title: {f:colr} is not a CSS property; did you mean {e:color}?

provide.how: wutu_parse.utu:254 is_css_property checks only the shape of the name. Add a table of known CSS properties (accepting custom --names and vendor prefixes) and did-you-mean against it.

feasibility.mechanism_check: Against a CSS property table, colr → color is distance 1; no other property (e.g. cols is not CSS) is within 1, and the next nearest are farther.

what: an element whose closing brace is missing

ideal.title: Element {f:section} is never closed

provide.how: Already reported at the head; add the end of the body as a related span (dsl_inner_end).

ideal.title: {c:for items} needs a capture such as {e:|item|}

ideal.title: Two elements are aliased {f:label}, so {f:label} here is ambiguous
notes: Give each a distinct alias, or reference it inside its own subtree.

what: an interpolated expression with a syntax error

feasibility.changed: Dropped the fix: deleting the + is one option among completing the operand.

what: a DOM property assignment without a value

ideal.title: The property {f:.value} has no value

provide.how: wutu_parse.utu:1030 has the right text ("a property takes a value") but `.value;` is first tried as a class-only head (:775). Check for ".name" followed by ";" before the element-head branch.

what: a text string missing its closing quote

ideal.title: This string is never closed

provide.how: Reported at the opening quote; span to the end of the line and add the fix closing it before the first ";".

feasibility.changed: Dropped the fix: where the string should end is a guess.

what: assigning an I32 to an input element value (a Str)

ideal.title: {c:.value} wants a {e:Str}, but {f:items.len()} is an {f:I32}

provide.how: The Wutu expansion emits the property assignment twice (create and update paths), so the mismatch is reported on two generated nodes. Dedup by mapped span (as for 76); the property's declared type is known from the foreign binding and gives the expected span.

what: a CSS property written with a space instead of a hyphen

ideal.title: {f:background color} is not a CSS property; did you mean {e:background-color}?

provide.how: wutu_parse.utu fails "invalid CSS property" at one character. Span the head text up to ":" and, when replacing spaces with hyphens yields a known property (the table from 90), propose it.

feasibility.mechanism_check: Against the CSS property table, "background color" → background-color is distance 1 (space → hyphen), the unique candidate.

what: a :hover selector block whose last declaration has no semicolon

ideal.title: The CSS declaration {f:color: red} has no semicolon

provide.how: Reported at the closing brace; move the span back to the declaration just read and add the insertion.

feasibility.mechanism_check: At the } closing the :hover block after `color: red`, the parser expects exactly `;`.

what: a lookup returns null and the caller unwraps it with `orelse fatal`

ideal.title: {c:orelse fatal} reached: {f:find_user(2)} returned null
notes: {c:orelse fatal} stops the program when the left side is null; {c:orelse} with a value falls back instead.

provide.how: check_orelse (selfhost/control.utu) lowers `x orelse fatal` to a bare Op.RefAsNonNull, so V8 reports "dereferencing a null pointer" with no location. It needs a trap-site table: while encoding code (wasm.utu encode_code) the encoder records each trapping instruction's and each call's byte offset with the source node it came from (w_node in wasm.utu keeps no source node today, so a parallel w_src vec, set from check_expr's current node, is needed), shipped beside host_json in the spec; the CLI parses `wasm-function[N]:0xOFF` out of error.stack and maps every wasm frame to file:line:col, dropping cli/ and src/runtime/ frames, with the site's kind recorded as orelse-fatal and the left operand's source text, so the title can name find_user(2); plus a name section, which wasm.utu already writes (encode_names, behind set_debug_names; compiler.js takes debugNames) but cli/utu.mjs never asks for, so frames read wasm-function[N] instead of the function.

feasibility.changed: Dropped the fix: orelse "unknown" invents a fallback value; the note already names orelse with a value.

what: an @es binding declared to return Str returns null (a missing DOM attribute, say)

ideal.title: {n:read_setting} returned null, but its type says {e:Str}

lines.text: let read_setting: fun(Str) Str = @es/\ (key) => ({ theme: "dark" })[key] ?? null \/;

notes: A value from {c:@es} is checked against the binding's type as it enters utu; declare {c:?Str} if null is possible.

provide.how: Today null passes the boundary into a (ref extern) Str slot and traps later at `.len()` as "illegal cast at length". The compiler knows the binding name, its declared result type, and its declaration span (selfhost/foreign.utu); it should put them in spec.es beside each generated __es_N field so importObjectFromGlue (src/runtime/host-imports.js) wraps the body and checks the result (null, typeof) before returning, throwing a utu boundary error that carries the binding and the call site (the call site from the trap-site table).

feasibility.changed: Dropped the fix: making the binding ?Str only moves the error to lang.len() (fixcheck other); no mechanism yields a working one-line edit. The note keeps the ?Str option.

what: an @es binding declared to return I32 returns a string

ideal.title: {n:count} returned the string {f:"12"}, but its type says {e:I32}
notes: utu does not convert JavaScript values for you; return a number from the {c:@es} body, or declare the binding {c:Str}.

provide.how: The JS API's ToWebAssemblyValue silently coerces "12" to 12 for an i32 result, so nothing fails. feasibility.changed: Removed the found mark on "12" inside the @es body (the compiler does not analyse JavaScript); dropped the Number(...) fix, which invents JS code.

notes: Indexes run from 0 to {c:xs.len() - 1}.

what: reading a Buffer at an index past its length (but inside its capacity)

ideal.title: Buffer index {f:5} is past its length {e:3}
notes: A Buffer's length counts what was pushed; the spare capacity beyond it holds no values.

provide.how: std/Buffer.utu guards indexing with `if checks() and (i < 0 or i >= self.length) { fatal; }`, and checks() (@ir <ir-safe-checks/>) is false unless --safe, so a read inside the capacity returns a stale slot and one past it traps in array.get; under --safe the bare `fatal` reads "unreachable". The check should be on in run and test builds (one compare), and std needs a fatal that carries a message and operands (say `fatal "Buffer index {i} is past its length {n}"`, lowered to a host import call before unreachable), attributed to the caller's site so std frames fold into the user's call. The location comes from the trap-site table. The "length is now 3" mark is static: the last push on the same local before the index. Marks that said where a runtime value came from (a push, a literal, an argument) were removed: the trap knows only its own site and the stack. The --safe check in std/Buffer.utu get_index has i and length in hand; it must pass them to a host import before fatal, and must be kept in non-safe builds for this to trap at all.

feasibility.changed: Removed "length is now 3" on the last push (runtime history) and the b[b.len() - 1] fix (invents the index).

The check should be on in run and test builds (one compare), and std needs a fatal that carries a message and operands (say `fatal "Buffer index {i} is past its length {n}"`, lowered to a host import call before unreachable), attributed to the caller's site so std frames fold into the user's call. notes: Check {c:b.len() > 0} before popping.
